items.zh: 二勝處 · 內有色相外觀色多
parent: The Eight Stations of Mastery: Naming, Stages, and Mastering a Small Object
八勝處 · 釋名 · 階位 · 勝知見一二

zh: 二、內有色相，外觀色多，若好若醜，是名勝知勝見者。行者觀心既調，爾時不滅內骨人，更於定中廣觀外色，所謂諦觀一死屍乃至十百千萬，一國土乃至十百千萬國，一閻浮提乃至一四天下等，皆見悉是死屍。若觀一胮脹時，悉見一切胮脹，乃至壞、血污、膿爛、青瘀、剝落亦如是。行者既廣見死屍不淨，心甚厭惡，次當諦觀一死屍脫除皮骨，但見白骨，如是乃至一切死屍悉除皮肉，皆見白骨遍滿世界。此觀如《禪經》廣明，是中應具說。
en: Second, "form within, contemplating much form without, whether good or ill — this is named superior knowledge, superior vision": the practitioner's own contemplating mind now regulated, at this time one does not extinguish the internal figure of bone, but, further, within concentration, broadly contemplates external form — namely, closely contemplating a single corpse, and then ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand; a single land, and then ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand lands; a single Jambudvīpa, and then a single four-continent world-system — all seen, entirely, as corpses. Contemplating a single body swollen, one sees every body swollen at once; and so, too, with decay, blood-smearing, festering, livid discoloration, and peeling away, each in turn.

The practitioner, having broadly seen the corpses' own impurity, the mind deeply wearied and revolted, next closely contemplates a single corpse stripped of its skin and bone, seeing only white bone — and so, too, all the way through every corpse, each stripped of skin and flesh, until white bone is seen filling the whole world. This contemplation is explained at length in the Dhyāna Sūtra, and should be given here in full.

zh: 行者外骨觀既成，復當定心諦觀內身白骨，鍊使明淨，如珂如貝。當自觀骨時，見外一切骨人悉皆起立，行行相對羅列，舉手而來。行者於三昧中即知此諸骨人皆是隨想而來，無有定實，心不驚怖。復當心默念，訶此骨人：「咄！汝諸骨人，從何而來！」如是訶時，悉見骨人悉還躄地，如是或至多反。行者深觀內骨，即見光明普照十方，一切骨人為光所照，悉亦明淨。此觀成時，於一切怨、親、中人及諸好醜，其心平等，無有愛恚，是名若好若醜勝知勝見。好醜勝知見義如前說。
en: The practitioner, the contemplation of external bone now accomplished, should, further, with the mind in concentration, closely contemplate the internal body's own white bone, refining it to bright purity, like agate, like shell. Contemplating his own bones in this way, he sees every external figure of bone rise up together, arrayed in rows facing one another, raising their hands and approaching. The practitioner, within samādhi, thereby knows that all these figures of bone arise entirely in accordance with his own thought, possessing no fixed reality at all, the mind unafraid and untroubled. He should, further, silently reflect, reproaching these figures of bone: "Ha! You figures of bone — from where have you come?" Reproaching them in this way, he sees every figure of bone collapse back to the ground at once — this may happen many times over.

The practitioner, deeply contemplating the internal bone, thereupon sees light illuminating the ten directions everywhere, every figure of bone illuminated by this light, all alike bright and pure. Once this contemplation is accomplished, toward every enemy, every loved one, and every neutral person, and every mark of good and ill alike, the mind is equal throughout, free of both love and hatred — this is named "whether good or ill, superior knowledge, superior vision." The sense of superior knowledge and vision regarding good and ill is as already explained above.

zh: 復次，行者住此觀中，能見一骨人，遍四天下皆是骨人，是名為多。還復攝念，觀一骨人，故名勝知勝見。隨意五欲男女、淨潔相中能勝故，故名勝處。又能善調觀心，雖知能觀之心性無所有，而於緣中自在迴轉，觀諸境界無有障閡，故名勝處。有義如《摩訶衍》中廣說。復次，有師言：「若但觀一切人，見不淨白骨，是名少；若作大不淨觀，是名多。」大不淨觀者，為破一切處貪愛故。何謂一切觀？觀象、馬、牛、羊六畜飛禽走獸之屬，悉見為死屍胮脹。復次，觀飲食皆如蟲如糞，衣服絹布猶如爛皮爛肉之段，臭處可惡。錢財金寶如毒蛇蚖，斯須死變，臭爛不淨，穀米如臭死蟲，宅舍、田園、國土、城邑、大地、山川、林藪，皆悉爛壞，臭處不淨，流溢滂沱，乃至見白骨狼藉，一切世間不淨，如此甚可厭患。行者於三昧中，隨觀即見，迴轉自在，能破一切世間好醜、愛憎、貪憂煩惱，故名「內有色相，外觀色多，若好若醜，勝知勝見」。
en: Furthermore, the practitioner, abiding within this contemplation, is able to see a single figure of bone, and then see the whole four-continent world filled entirely with figures of bone — this is named "much." Gathering the mind once more, contemplating a single figure of bone again — hence this, too, is named superior knowledge, superior vision: able to master, at will, the five desires, whether male or female, whether pure or unblemished in mark — hence this is named a station of mastery. And, further, one is thereby able to skillfully master the contemplating mind itself — though knowing that the very nature of the mind able to contemplate possesses nothing at all, one nonetheless turns freely within its own object, contemplating every realm without any obstruction whatsoever — hence this, too, is named a station of mastery. This sense is explained at greater length in the Mahāyāna treatise.

Furthermore, there is a master who says: "Should one merely contemplate every person, seeing the impure white bone alone, this is named little; should one perform the great contemplation of impurity, this is named much." The great contemplation of impurity is for the sake of breaking through craving and attachment toward every possible object. What is meant by contemplating everything? Contemplating elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and every kind of the six domestic animals, and every bird and beast, all seen as corpses, swollen. Furthermore, contemplating food and drink as though it were worms or excrement, and clothing, silk, and cloth as though they were strips of rotten skin and rotten flesh, foul and abhorrent. Money, wealth, gold, and jewels seen as poisonous snakes and vipers, transforming in an instant into death, stinking and rotten, impure; grain and rice seen as stinking, dead worms; houses, fields and gardens, one's own land, cities and towns, the great earth, mountains, rivers, and forests, all, alike, rotting and decaying, foul and impure, overflowing and pouring forth — and, further still, seeing white bones scattered everywhere, the whole world impure — a matter, in this way, utterly to be wearied of and abhorred. The practitioner, within samādhi, sees whatever he contemplates at will, turning freely, able thereby to break through every worldly good and ill, love and hatred, craving and sorrowful affliction — hence this is named "form within, contemplating much form without, whether good or ill, superior knowledge, superior vision."

zh: 問：世間資生既不淨，悉是皮肉筋骨之法，云何悉見不淨爛壞？答曰：此為得解之道，心力轉變，非實觀也。所以者何？一切非實是淨，淨倒力故，遂悉見淨而生貪愛。一切雖非悉不淨，今不淨觀智慧力皆見不淨，破諸煩惱，復有何過？譬如劫燒火起，一切大地有情、無情，若干種類，皆成火焰，以火力故。今以不淨心觀一切世間，悉見不淨，亦如神通之人轉瓦石為金玉，當知諸法有何定性？彼師如是明。第二勝處，深思此意，義理觀行，悉可依用也。
en: Question: since the world's own resources for living are, in every case, dharmas of skin, flesh, tendon, and bone, and thus already impure, how can they all be seen as impure and decaying? Answer: this is the path of understanding attained, the mind's own power transforming appearances — it is not a contemplation of what is literally real. Why is this? Nothing is, in reality, entirely pure; through the power of the inverted view of purity, one comes to see everything as pure and thereby gives rise to craving and attachment toward it. Though nothing is, in reality, entirely impure either, here, through the power of the contemplation of impurity's own wisdom, everything is seen as impure, breaking through every affliction — what fault, then, could there be in this? It is like the fire that arises at the eon's own burning: every being and every non-sentient thing upon the whole earth, of whatever kind, all alike become flame, through the very power of that fire. Here, too, using the mind that contemplates impurity to contemplate the whole world, one sees it, in every case, as impure — just as a person of supernormal power is able to transform tile and stone into gold and jewels. One should know, then: what fixed nature could any dharma possibly possess? This master explains it in just this way, and, deeply reflecting on this sense with respect to the second station of mastery, its own principle and contemplative practice may, in every case, be relied upon and put to use.

The escalation from a single corpse to an entire world filled with corpses, and then the alternate master's even more radical extension — every possession, every food, every animal, every city seen as equally impure — pushes the nine contemplations' original single-body meditation to a civilizational scale. The closing question-and-answer is philosophically the most interesting moment in the whole section: the text openly concedes this is "not a contemplation of what is literally real," a deliberate distortion used as a corrective against an opposite, equally unreal distortion (seeing the world as desirable) — the same logic as the eon-ending fire that turns everything on earth into flame by its own power, or the supernormal power that turns tile into gold. Neither the ordinary view nor the corrective view is being presented as ultimately true; both are provisional, matched to what the mind needs at a given stage.

items.en: The Remaining Stations of Mastery, and How They Lead Toward the Path
items.zh: 三四勝處 · 青黃赤白四勝處 · 趣道
parent: The Eight Stations of Mastery: Naming, Stages, and Mastering a Small Object
八勝處 · 釋名 · 階位 · 勝知見一二

zh: 次明第三、第四勝處，觀行方法不異於前，但以內無色相為異。滅內色方法，前二背捨初門說。今行者為欲界煩惱歎破故，於第二禪中重修此二勝處，對治除滅下地結使，令無遺餘，亦以重轉變觀道，令利熟增明，牢固不失，工力轉勝也。
en: Next, clarifying the third and fourth stations of mastery: the contemplative method here differs not at all from what came before, differing only in taking "no form within" as its own mark. The method for extinguishing internal form is already explained at the opening gate of the second detachment above. Here, because the desire realm's own afflictions are difficult to break through, the practitioner once more cultivates these two stations of mastery within the second dhyāna, serving as an antidote to eliminate the lower stage's own fetters entirely, leaving nothing whatsoever behind, and, further, repeatedly transforming the contemplative path itself, so that it grows ever sharper, more mature, and more illuminating, firm and never lost, its own effort and power growing ever more excellent.

zh: 次釋青、黃、赤、白四勝處者，行者不受三禪身證之樂，入第四禪時，念慧清淨，四色轉更光顯，如妙寶光明，勝於前色，故名勝處。復次，行者於四禪中用不動智慧鍊此四色，少能多，多能少，轉變自在，欲見即見，欲滅即滅，故名勝處。復次，行者於三昧中見是勝色，結漏未斷，或時法愛心生，為斷法愛，諦觀此色，知從心起，譬如幻師觀所幻色，知從心生，則不生著，是時背捨變名勝處。
en: Next, explaining the four stations of mastery of blue-green, yellow, red, and white: the practitioner, no longer accepting the third dhyāna's own happiness realized in the body, upon entering the fourth dhyāna, mindfulness and wisdom now pure, these four colors turn ever more radiant and clear, like the light of some wondrous jewel, surpassing the colors that came before — hence this is named a station of mastery. Furthermore, the practitioner, within the fourth dhyāna, using unshakeable wisdom, refines these four colors, able to make the small great and the great small, transforming them freely at will, seeing them the moment he wishes to see them, and dissolving them the moment he wishes to dissolve them — hence this, too, is named a station of mastery. Furthermore, the practitioner, seeing this very superior color within samādhi, the fetters and contaminants not yet severed, may, at times, give rise to a mind of attachment to the dharma itself; in order to sever this attachment to the dharma, one closely contemplates this very color, knowing it to arise from the mind — like a magician contemplating his own conjured form, knowing it to arise from the mind, and thereby giving rise to no attachment toward it. At this time, detachment is renamed a station of mastery.

zh: 第四、明趣道之相，亦為三意：一者、先用勝處調心，然後具足修習超越等法，發真無漏，證三乘道；二者、此八勝處具足成就，深入四諦真觀，第四禪中發真無漏，具足三十四心，斷三界結，證三乘道；三者、自有行人得初勝處，入初禪時，厭畏心重，即作念言：「我今何用事中諸禪？但須疾取涅槃。」作此念已，即於此地深觀四諦、十二因緣、中道、實相，若發無漏，即證三乘聖果也。下七勝處亦當一一如是分別。菩薩摩訶薩雖知諸法畢竟空寂，憐愍一切眾生故，深修勝處。於勝處中發大神通，摧伏天魔，破諸外道，度脫眾生，當知勝處即是菩薩摩訶衍。
en: Fourth, clarifying the mark of how the stations of mastery lead toward the path: this, too, has three senses.

First, one first uses the stations of mastery to regulate the mind, and only afterward becomes complete in cultivating the samādhi of transcendence and the rest, true undefilement thereby arising, and the path of the three vehicles realized. Second, one completes the accomplishment of these eight stations of mastery and penetrates deeply into the true contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, true undefilement arising within the fourth dhyāna itself, complete with the thirty-four moments of mind, severing the fetters of the three realms, and realizing the path of the three vehicles. Third, there is the case of a practitioner who, obtaining the first station of mastery upon entering the first dhyāna, the mind heavy with weariness and dread, thereupon reflects: "What use, now, do I have for these many dhyānas amid such concrete matters? I need only swiftly seize hold of nirvāṇa itself." Having reflected in this way, he thereupon, at this very stage, deeply contemplates the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, the middle way, and true reality — should the undefiled arise, he thereby realizes the noble fruit of the three vehicles directly. The remaining seven stations of mastery should each, in turn, be distinguished in this same way.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, though knowing that every dharma is, in the end, empty and still, out of compassion for every sentient being, deeply cultivates the stations of mastery. Within the stations of mastery, great supernormal powers arise, subduing the heavenly māras, breaking through every non-Buddhist teaching, and delivering sentient beings across. One should know, then, that the stations of mastery are themselves precisely the bodhisattva's own Mahāyāna.

The four colored stations of mastery mark a genuine shift in the whole sequence's own object: after the first four stations of mastery, worked largely through corpses and bones (though the eight colors of light have been present since the first detachment), the fourth dhyāna's practitioner now takes pure, jewel-like color itself as the object to refine, with an explicit warning against the new risk this creates — attachment to the dharma itself (法愛), the beautiful meditative object becoming a subtler trap than the corpse ever was. The magician-and-conjured-form simile used to break that attachment recurs across this entire treatise as the standard antidote whenever a meditative attainment risks becoming an object of craving in its own right. The three routes to the path closing this section again refuse to prescribe one single sequence, echoing the same structural generosity already given for the nine contemplations, the ten perceptions, and the eight forms of detachment before it.

quiz.q: How does the second station broadly contemplate external form?
options: keeping the inner bones, one sees corpses multiplying to fill the world, then all as white bones
quiz.why: Without extinguishing the inner bones, one sees one corpse, then thousands, a land, Jambudvīpa, a whole world-system, all corpses, then all as white bones.

quiz.q: When the outer skeletons rise and approach in samādhi, how does the practitioner respond?
options: knowing they arise from thought, unafraid, one rebukes them and they collapse
quiz.why: One knows the skeletons come only from one's own thought, without fixed reality, and is not afraid; rebuking them silently, they all collapse back to the ground.

quiz.q: What is the "great impurity contemplation" for, and what does it contemplate?
options: to break craving everywhere; seeing animals, food, clothes, wealth, houses, lands as rotting
quiz.why: It breaks craving toward every object: animals, food, clothing, wealth, houses, lands, and mountains are all seen as rotting and impure.

quiz.q: Asked how all worldly things can be seen as rotting, how does the text answer and with what simile?
options: it is deliberate contemplation, the mind transforming appearances, not literal; like the eon-fire turning all to flame, or turning stone to gold
quiz.why: It is a path of deliberate understanding, the mind transforming appearances, not literal seeing; as the eon-fire turns everything to flame and a person with powers turns stone to gold, dharmas have no fixed nature.

quiz.q: How do the third and fourth stations differ from the first two?
options: the method is the same, differing only in having no form within
quiz.why: The method is the same as before, differing only in having no form within; they are cultivated again in the second dhyāna to remove lower fetters.

quiz.q: Why are the blue, yellow, red, and white stations called stations of mastery?
options: in the fourth dhyāna the colors shine brighter, and with unmoving wisdom one transforms them at will
quiz.why: In the fourth dhyāna, with pure mindfulness and wisdom, the four colors shine brighter than before; refining them with unmoving wisdom one makes small large and large small at will.

quiz.q: To sever attachment to the superior colors, how does one contemplate, and with what simile?
options: seeing the color arise from mind, like a magician seeing his conjured forms
quiz.why: To sever attachment, one sees the color arising from the mind, like a magician who knows his conjured forms come from his mind; then detachment is renamed mastery.

quiz.q: In the third way the stations lead to the path, what does the practitioner think on attaining the first?
options: "What use are these dhyānas? I need only seize nirvāṇa," then contemplates the truths and the middle way
quiz.why: Heavy with weariness, he thinks he has no use for these dhyānas and need only seize nirvāṇa, and contemplates the truths, links, middle way, and true reality right there.

quiz.q: In the second way, how many moments of mind are complete when the undefiled arises in the fourth dhyāna?
quiz.why: Complete in the eight stations and contemplating the Four Truths, the undefiled arises in the fourth dhyāna with thirty-four moments of mind, severing the fetters.
